Find the least distance $d$ between the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+3$ and the point $(4,3).$ Do not round the answer.

$d=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(4,3)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-4)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x}+3-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x})^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+16+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-6 & =0 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0,$ so $x=3$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=3$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(3)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(3)} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}-6(3)+16} \\  & =\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$
